passage:
Dear Chetan,

I'm writing this instead of saying it in the group because I didn't want you to feel singled out.

When we split the survey project, I gave you the data tables since you're quicker with spreadsheets than any of us. It's been ten days and the sheet is still mostly blank. I'm not angry. I'm a bit worried, because the others are waiting on those numbers for their sections.

Is something getting in the way? Too much work from other subjects, something at home, or was the task unclear? If it's the last one, that's on me.

Can we meet Thursday after class for twenty minutes? We can break it into smaller parts, or I can move some to Ruchi.

Either way, you're still on this team.

Vinita

qa.q: When did Vinita suggest meeting Chetan?
qa.a: Vinita suggested Thursday after class, for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What is Vinita worried about, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Vinita is worried the rest of the team is stuck waiting for the numbers; the letter says so directly and still says Vinita is not angry.

qa.q: Which parts of Vinita's letter make it kind but still firm?
qa.a: Vinita asks what is getting in the way, owns a possible share of the problem, and offers concrete options instead of blaming Chetan.

qa.q: If you were Chetan, how might this letter feel?
qa.a: It could feel embarrassing but also relieving, because it gives a private way to explain and a clear chance to fix it. 🙏

grounding: Shows a student leader who divided work handling a teammate's lag with kindness and a concrete plan.

passage: So, yeah, I'm Naveen, and I was the fest coordinator last year, and I thought leading meant doing everything myself. First week, I made one big list and told eight people to pick things. Chaos. Three people picked posters, nobody picked sponsors. After that I sat down and gave each person one clear job and a date. That part worked. The hard part was Jahnavi. She'd promised the stage plan and kept saying 'almost done'. I was annoyed, honestly. But instead of complaining in the group, I asked her for chai. Turned out her mother was in hospital and she was too embarrassed to say. We paired her with someone, and she still did the lighting beautifully. I learned the direction has to be clear, but people aren't machines.

qa.q: How many people did Naveen first ask to pick tasks from a list?
qa.a: Naveen asked eight people.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi likely feeling when she kept saying 'almost done'?
qa.a: She was probably stressed and embarrassed, because her mother was in hospital and she did not want to admit she was falling behind.

qa.q: Which of Naveen's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Giving each person one clear job and date removed confusion, and talking privately to Jahnavi uncovered the real problem.

qa.q: What would have changed if Naveen had complained about Jahnavi in the group?
qa.a: She might have felt shamed and hidden her situation even more, and the stage work could have stayed stuck.

grounding: Shows a young leader learning to set clear roles and to handle a struggling teammate privately and kindly.

passage: I'm Uday, and I was in Wasim's group for the robotics project. I'll tell you what I saw. On day one he drew the whole robot on the whiteboard and wrote our names next to parts: me on wiring, Soham on code, Parth on the frame. Nobody argued, because it was clear. Around week three Parth kept missing lab sessions. Some of us wanted to report him. Wasim didn't. He waited after class, walked Parth to the canteen, and they talked for a while. I don't know what was said. Next day Parth came with half the frame done and Wasim had quietly taken one small part off his list. Parth never missed again. Wasim looked tired that week, but he never once raised his voice.

qa.q: Which part of the robot did Uday work on?
qa.a: Uday was put on the wiring.

qa.q: What might Wasim have been thinking when he chose not to report Parth?
qa.a: He was probably concerned about why Parth kept missing sessions and wanted to understand before treating it as a discipline problem.

qa.q: What could other student leaders learn from how Wasim divided the work?
qa.a: Drawing the whole project and naming who owns each part makes roles clear from the start and avoids arguments.

qa.q: How might Parth have seen Wasim's approach?
qa.a: He likely felt given a fair chance instead of being exposed, which may be why he started showing up again.

grounding: Shows an observer describing a peer leader setting direction and handling underperformance quietly and kindly.

passage: Day 1: Farhan, chosen to lead the four-person robotics project, opened the meeting with, 'Goal: a working prototype in three weeks.' He wrote the tasks on the board and let each person pick one. Naveen chose the sensor wiring. Day 9: The wiring still wasn't done, and the others were grumbling in the group chat. Farhan was tempted to post something sharp. Instead he found Naveen in the canteen. 'The sensors are stuck. What's going on?' Naveen admitted he had never soldered before and was too embarrassed to say so. Farhan paired him with Riya for two evenings and moved the deadline for that part by three days, telling the team why. Day 19: The prototype rolled across the lab floor. Naveen demonstrated the sensor part to the professor, a little proudly.

qa.q: Which task did Naveen choose?
qa.a: The sensor wiring.

qa.q: Why hadn't Naveen told anyone about the wiring problem?
qa.a: He had never soldered before and felt too embarrassed to admit it.

qa.q: What did Farhan try instead of posting something sharp, and why did it work?
qa.a: He spoke to Naveen privately, found the real reason, paired him with Riya and openly adjusted the deadline, fixing the problem without shaming him.

qa.q: How might the rest of the team have seen Farhan's decision?
qa.a: They had been grumbling, but his explanation of the new deadline helped them understand it and trust how he handled things.

grounding: Shows a student leader setting a goal, dividing tasks and handling a teammate's underperformance kindly over three weeks.

passage: Ankita, you look exactly how I looked at twenty-one, when they made me supervisor of the packing line at the biscuit factory in Aurangabad. Four women, all older than me. For a month I did half their work myself because I was scared to tell them what to do. I went home aching, and they thought I didn't trust them. One of them, Rukmini, finally said, 'Jyoti madam, tell us the target and let us plan.' Oof. So I did. Every morning I said the day's number and asked who would take which part. When one lady kept falling behind, I asked her quietly, away from the others, and learned she couldn't read the small labels well. We moved her to cartons. See, leading isn't doing it all. It's giving direction and noticing people.

qa.q: What was Jyoti put in charge of at twenty-one?
qa.a: The packing line at the biscuit factory, supervising four women older than her.

qa.q: Why did Jyoti do half the work herself at first?
qa.a: She was scared to tell older women what to do.

qa.q: How did Jyoti handle the worker who kept falling behind?
qa.a: She asked her quietly, away from the others, learned she could not read the small labels well, and moved her to cartons.

qa.q: How did the women on the line see Jyoti doing their work?
qa.a: They thought she did not trust them, which is why Rukmini asked her simply to give the target.

grounding: A senior woman recalls learning to lead a small team by giving direction and handling a struggling worker kindly.
